narrativeReportMd:
# Practitioner R4-to-R6 breaking-change assessment

## Bottom line
R6 retains the same `Practitioner` resource identity, but there are material local migration risks. The hardest break is `Practitioner.communication`, which changed from a repeating `CodeableConcept` to a repeating backbone element with mandatory `language` and optional `preferred`. R6 also marks `active` as a modifier and adds modifier choice `deceased[x]`, both of which affect safe runtime processing.

## Scope
The report covers the local base Practitioner StructureDefinition in R4 4.0.1 and R6 6.0.0-ballot4. Inherited base-artifact changes visible in the snapshot are excluded, including DomainResource constraints and Resource/Element/Extension elements. Search parameters and PractitionerRole are follow-up artifacts, not Practitioner findings here.

## Main migration themes
1. Communication data needs both a structural transform and a semantic review. R4 `communication` values should be wrapped as R6 `communication.language`, but R6 text changes the intended meaning toward communicating with the practitioner and points patient-facing role-specific language publication to PractitionerRole.
2. Modifier handling becomes more important. `active` is now a modifier, and the new `deceased[x]` element is a modifier that cannot be safely dropped in mixed-version workflows.
3. R6 adds qualification lifecycle state with `qualification.status`, improving credentialing expressiveness but creating R6-to-R4 round-trip loss unless an extension is used.

## Highest-impact findings
High-impact findings are the communication representation break, `active` becoming a modifier, and the added `deceased[x]` modifier. The communication binding change and semantic redirection require human review because valid-looking transformations can still fail terminology validation or carry the wrong business meaning.

## Findings requiring human review
Human review is most important for language migration (`Practitioner.communication` versus `PractitionerRole.communication`), terminology cleanup for required BCP 47 language tags, and downgrade policy for `deceased[x]` and `qualification.status`.

## Backward-compatible design observations
Several changes could have been modeled through extensions to reduce R4/R6 wire-format breakage, especially `communication.preferred`, `deceased[x]`, and `qualification.status`. The R6 base additions are nevertheless plausible because they improve first-class semantics and safer generic processing.

## Follow-up analysis
A PractitionerRole comparison should verify the target for patient-facing communication languages. Terminology expansion for all-languages and qualification-status would improve confidence in binding-related impact.

summary.executiveSummaryMd: R6 Practitioner has one hard local instance-format break: `Practitioner.communication` changed from `CodeableConcept[]` to a backbone array. The main migration concerns are communication reshaping/semantics, required BCP 47 language validation, and new modifier/status handling for `active`, `deceased[x]`, and qualification status. The top uncertainty is terminology and official rationale because no live expansions or official diff were used.
summary.migrationThemesMd: Migrations should treat Practitioner communication as a special case rather than a simple same-path copy. R4 language CodeableConcepts must be wrapped into `communication.language`, checked against the R6 required all-languages binding, and reviewed for whether they belong on Practitioner or PractitionerRole. Runtime stacks must regenerate models and honor R6 modifier semantics for `active` and `deceased[x]`. Downgrade paths need extensions or documented loss for `deceased[x]`, `communication.preferred`, and `qualification.status`.
summary.confidenceSummaryMd: Confidence is high for structural, cardinality, datatype, reference target, and flag findings because they come directly from local R4 and R6 StructureDefinitions and package indexes. Confidence is medium for terminology prevalence and justification because no live terminology expansion, official diff, Jira item, or narrative page was consulted.

findings.title: Practitioner.communication changed from CodeableConcept to a BackboneElement with language and preferred children

oldState.summary: Optional repeating CodeableConcept directly on Practitioner.communication.

semanticText.short: A language the practitioner can use in patient communication
semanticText.definition: A language the practitioner can use in patient communication.

oldState.narrativeMd: In R4, each `Practitioner.communication` array item was itself a `CodeableConcept`, so JSON contained `coding` and/or `text` directly under `communication[]`.

newState.summary: Optional repeating BackboneElement; language is required within each repetition and preferred is optional.

semanticText.short: A language which may be used to communicate with the practitioner
semanticText.definition: A language which may be used to communicate with the practitioner, often for correspondence/administrative purposes.

newState.narrativeMd: In R6, `Practitioner.communication[]` is a backbone object. The language code lives in mandatory child `Practitioner.communication.language` and a new optional boolean child `preferred` can be present.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The element id and path remain `Practitioner.communication`, but the type changed and the R6 differential adds child elements under the same path.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is a direct wire-format and validation break for R4-to-R6. An R4 instance with `communication[0].coding` is no longer shaped like the R6 backbone element and must be transformed to `communication[0].language.coding`. Code generators also change the property type from `CodeableConcept[]` to a component/backbone class array. In the reverse direction, `communication.language` can map back to R4, but R6 `communication.preferred` has no base R4 field and would need an extension or be lost.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Incorrect transformation can drop language preferences or cause systems to mis-handle communication needs for practitioners.

justification.inferredGoal: Add per-language preference and prepare for richer communication metadata while keeping the repeating communication concept.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain the R4 CodeableConcept shape and add preference support through a companion base element or core-defined extension.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The R6 backbone shape addresses a real modeling gap: a bare repeating `CodeableConcept` cannot carry per-language metadata such as `preferred` as a first-class base element. The change is still a hard wire-format break, so it is only probably justified absent official rationale. The best less-breaking base design would avoid invalidating R4 `communication` arrays, but it would leave implementations with both legacy language entries and richer preference-bearing entries to reconcile.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking R6 design could have kept `Practitioner.communication` as the R4 repeating `CodeableConcept` and added a separate optional preference mechanism, such as a companion base element identifying preferred languages or a core-defined extension on each communication CodeableConcept. That preserves most R4 instances. It is only a partial alternative because per-language facts could become duplicated or inconsistent, old and new representations might persist indefinitely, and generic R6 clients would have weaker ability to validate, search, and process preference consistently.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: This would preserve old JSON but create duplicate or split same-resource representations and weaker first-class validation/search support.

evidence.detail: R6 adds mandatory child language with cardinality 1..1 and type CodeableConcept.
R6 adds optional child preferred with type boolean.

examples.examplesMd: The examples are minimal fragments showing the changed JSON shape. A full migration wraps each R4 `CodeableConcept` as R6 `communication.language`; `preferred` requires a policy or extension when mapping back to R4.

findings.narrativeMd: `Practitioner.communication` kept the same path but no longer has the same datatype or JSON shape. R4 clients and generated classes that expect an array of `CodeableConcept` will fail against R6 data, and R4 instances must be rewritten before R6 validation. This is the highest-confidence hard break in the local Practitioner definition.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Old-valid/new-invalid: yes. R4 JSON with `communication[].coding` or `communication[].text` directly under the repetition does not satisfy the R6 backbone content model. R6-to-R4 is partially representable by unwrapping `language`, but `preferred` has no R4 base slot.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Transform each R4 `communication` item to an R6 object with `language` equal to the old CodeableConcept. Decide whether any local extensions or business rules can populate `preferred`. For reverse conversion, unwrap `language` and preserve `preferred` in an extension if it matters. Update generated models, serializers, FHIRPath expressions, and tests that address `Practitioner.communication.coding` directly.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The break was partly avoidable if preference had been modeled as an extension, but a backbone element is a reasonable base-model choice once per-language metadata is required. The tradeoff is a non-compatible wire-format change for a previously simple repeating datatype.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: The same path name can hide the break in shallow diffs; type-aware comparison is required.

findings.title: Practitioner communication language binding strengthened from preferred languages to required all-languages

oldState.summary: Preferred binding to common languages; non-listed CodeableConcepts could still validate.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: The R4 binding also carried a maxValueSet extension pointing at all-languages, but the enforceable binding strength on the element was preferred.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 validators could warn about codes outside the preferred language set, but base validation did not require a CodeableConcept coding from that value set.

newState.summary: Required binding to all IETF BCP 47 language tags for mandatory communication.language.

binding.description: IETF language tag for a human language

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: The local ValueSet compose includes `urn:ietf:bcp:47`; no live terminology expansion was performed.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 requires the communication language CodeableConcept to satisfy the all-languages value set.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The R6 `language` child contains the CodeableConcept that occupied `Practitioner.communication` in R4.

impact.impactRationaleMd: After the structural migration, a CodeableConcept that was valid in R4 because the binding was only preferred can become invalid in R6 if it lacks a coding in the required all-languages value set. Text-only language entries and local/non-BCP-47 coding systems are the main risk.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: The risk is primarily validation and interoperability rather than direct clinical safety, but lost or rejected language data can affect communication workflows.

justification.inferredGoal: Make practitioner communication languages computably constrained to IETF BCP 47 tags.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep the base binding preferred or extensible and require BCP 47 only through profiles, warnings, or best-practice guidance.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Requiring `all-languages` gives R6 a clear interoperable language-code contract, and the R6 element comments still acknowledge that some systems store language as free text. Because the R4 binding was only preferred, strict required binding can invalidate migrated legacy text-only or locally coded entries. A less-breaking path exists, but it would not provide the same base-level conformance strength.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The less-breaking design would retain the R4 preferred binding, or at most move to a softer constraint such as extensible binding plus best-practice warnings, while letting implementation guides require BCP 47 where appropriate. That would preserve more R4-valid data during migration. It is only partial because base R6 validators and generic clients would no longer be able to rely on every `communication.language` carrying a code from the required all-languages value set.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Less disruptive for text/local codes, but materially weakens the uniform base guarantee that communication languages use BCP 47.

evidence.detail: R4 binding strength is preferred and valueSet is languages.
R6 binding strength is required and valueSet is all-languages version 6.0.0-ballot4.

communication.text: Primary clinic language recorded as free text

examples.examplesMd: The old fragment is valid against a preferred binding but may fail R6 required-binding validation after wrapping because it lacks a coding in the required value set.

findings.narrativeMd: The language binding is not merely versioned; its strength increased from preferred to required and the required value set is the all-languages BCP 47 value set. This can turn previously acceptable free-text or locally coded communication languages into validation failures during R6 migration.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Old-valid/new-invalid is possible after the shape transform. A strict R6 terminology validator can reject a migrated `communication.language` CodeableConcept that does not contain a coding in the required value set. No reverse representability issue is created by the binding itself because R4 can carry the CodeableConcept, but R4 semantics would not enforce the R6 requirement.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Normalize communication languages to IETF BCP 47 where possible before or during migration. Keep original local text/codings as additional CodeableConcept content or extensions when needed, but include at least one valid BCP 47 coding for R6. Test text-only, local-code, common-language, and regional-tag cases with a terminology server.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The stronger binding improves computability but could have been introduced less disruptively through guidance or profiles. The base-model strengthening is more interoperable but imposes data cleanup on legacy R4 instances.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Confidence is medium rather than high because no live expansion or official terminology diff was run.

findings.title: Practitioner.communication semantic focus changed from patient communication to communicating with the practitioner

oldState.summary: Communication described languages the practitioner can use in patient communication.

semanticText.short: A language the practitioner can use in patient communication
semanticText.definition: A language the practitioner can use in patient communication.
semanticText.requirements: Knowing which language a practitioner speaks can help in facilitating communication with patients.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 framed the element around the practitioner speaking with patients.

newState.summary: Communication describes languages used to communicate with the practitioner; patient-facing languages are directed to PractitionerRole.communication.

semanticText.short: A language which may be used to communicate with the practitioner
semanticText.definition: A language which may be used to communicate with the practitioner, often for correspondence/administrative purposes. The PractitionerRole.communication property should be used for publishing the languages that a practitioner is able to communicate with patients (on a per Organization/Role basis).
semanticText.comment: If no language is specified, this implies that the default local language is spoken.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 narrows/reorients the base Practitioner element toward correspondence or administrative communication with the practitioner and points patient-facing capability to PractitionerRole.

facts.oldValue: A language the practitioner can use in patient communication.
facts.newValue: A language which may be used to communicate with the practitioner, often for correspondence/administrative purposes.
PractitionerRole.communication should be used for patient-facing language publication.
Absence implies default local language is spoken.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The same element path is retained, but its definition and comment materially redirect intended use.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The JSON may validate after structural transformation, but the business meaning can be wrong. R4 data often interpreted as patient-language capability should not automatically remain on Practitioner in R6 if it is role-, organization-, or patient-facing; R6 text directs that use to PractitionerRole.communication.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Misplacing language capability can affect scheduling, directories, and patient matching to language-compatible clinicians.

justification.inferredGoal: Separate practitioner administrative correspondence language from role-specific patient communication capability.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Preserve the R4 patient-communication meaning and add separate role-specific or administrative-language guidance/elements.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The R6 goal is conceptually reasonable: patient-facing language capability often depends on role, organization, or service context, while Practitioner can carry correspondence language for the person. Changing the meaning of an existing path is disruptive because structurally valid migrated data can still say the wrong thing. A less-breaking design could have staged the separation, but the tradeoff is persistent ambiguity.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking design could have kept the R4 `Practitioner.communication` meaning for patient communication, added clearer guidance that `PractitionerRole.communication` is preferred for role-specific publication, and introduced any administrative/correspondence language as a separate optional element or extension. This would preserve old semantics for existing instances. It is only partial because consumers would then face duplicate or overlapping language fields, uncertain precedence between Practitioner and PractitionerRole, and a longer-lived deprecated representation.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Avoids semantic surprise for old data, but leaves overlapping locations and ambiguity about global versus role-specific language capability.

evidence.detail: R4 defines the element as a language the practitioner can use in patient communication.
R6 defines the element as a language used to communicate with the practitioner and refers patient communication to PractitionerRole.communication.

examples.examplesMd: This illustrative split shows an administrative/default language on Practitioner and a patient-facing service language on PractitionerRole. The exact target depends on local source semantics.

findings.narrativeMd: This is a semantic/conformance change rather than a pure validation rule. Blindly wrapping every R4 communication CodeableConcept into R6 `communication.language` can produce R6-valid data that conveys the wrong thing if the original value meant languages the practitioner can use with patients in a role-specific context.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: A structurally migrated instance can still validate in R6, so this is not usually an old-valid/new-invalid issue. The compatibility problem is semantic: old patient-communication data may need relocation or duplication into PractitionerRole, and R6 data using the new correspondence meaning may be misleading if read by an R4 system as patient-communication capability.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Classify existing `Practitioner.communication` values by business meaning. Keep administrative/correspondence language on Practitioner; move or copy role-specific patient language capability to PractitionerRole.communication where that role resource is available. Add manual review for provider directories and scheduling workflows that use language matching.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change improves conceptual separation but could have been made less disruptive with deprecation guidance and a transition period. Because the same path remains, semantic migration rules are more important than simple field mapping.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: A full PractitionerRole assessment should verify the corresponding target element and its shape across versions.

findings.title: Practitioner.active became a modifier element in R6

oldState.summary: Optional boolean active element; not marked as a modifier.

semanticText.definition: Whether this practitioner's record is in active use.
semanticText.meaningWhenMissing: This resource is generally assumed to be active if no value is provided for the active element

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 allowed the element but did not flag it as changing how the resource must be interpreted.

newState.summary: Same optional boolean, but isModifier is true with a reason tied to invalid/inactive records.

flags.isModifierReason: This element is labelled as a modifier because it is a status element that can indicate that a record should not be treated as valid

semanticText.definition: Whether this practitioner's record is in active use.
semanticText.meaningWhenMissing: This resource is generally assumed to be active if no value is provided for the active element

newState.narrativeMd: R6 requires consumers to treat `active` as modifier information that can affect whether the Practitioner record should be used.

facts.newValue: status element that can indicate that a record should not be treated as valid

impact.impactRationaleMd: The same instance value validates in both versions, but R6 changes conformance expectations for safe consumption. Generated models, summary views, and business logic that ignore modifier elements must now account for `active=false` before treating a Practitioner as usable.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Using inactive or erroneous practitioner records in directories, assignments, orders, or access workflows can have operational and safety consequences.

justification.inferredGoal: Align active/status handling with FHIR modifier semantics so consumers cannot safely ignore inactive or invalid records.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: No equally effective less-breaking base design was identified; narrative guidance alone would not provide modifier semantics.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: `active` already meant the practitioner record might not be usable, including records created in error. Marking it as a modifier formalizes that existing safety and workflow meaning without changing instance wire format or cardinality. The compatibility cost is runtime/conformance behavior, and that cost is reasonable for a status element that can negate ordinary use of the resource.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The obvious alternative is to leave `active` as a non-modifier and strengthen the definition or comments. That is not a real backward-compatible alternative to the R6 goal because generic FHIR processors, generated models, and modifier-aware safety checks would still be permitted to ignore the element. No lower-breakage base design was identified that gives equivalent modifier-aware processing.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Keeping `isModifier=false` would preserve generated-model behavior but allow safety-relevant inactive status to be ignored by generic processors.

evidence.detail: R6 isModifier is true and includes an isModifierReason.

examples.examplesMd: The example remains syntactically valid; the change is that an R6 consumer must not ignore the modifier meaning of `active=false`.

findings.narrativeMd: `Practitioner.active` did not change cardinality or datatype, but its modifier flag changed. This is a runtime/conformance break for libraries and applications that classify modifier elements, generate special handling, or assume non-modifier data can be ignored without changing resource meaning.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: No ordinary R4 instance becomes invalid solely because of this flag. The compatibility break is behavioral: R6 processors must surface and honor the modifier semantics. R6 data is representable in R4 because the field already exists, but an R4 consumer will not learn from the R4 definition that this is a modifier.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Regenerate R6 models and update generic resource handling so `Practitioner.active` is included in modifier checks. Audit business rules that select practitioners for directories, assignment, prescribing, or authorization to ensure inactive records are excluded or reviewed according to policy.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Because the element already carried status semantics, marking it as a modifier is a justified conformance strengthening. There is no equally effective backward-compatible alternative other than weaker narrative guidance.

findings.title: R6 adds Practitioner.deceased[x] as an optional modifier choice

oldState.summary: No base R4 Practitioner deceased element.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 Practitioner had no local deceased field; systems used extensions, status conventions, or external records if they needed this fact.

newState.summary: Optional choice element deceased[x] with boolean and dateTime types; marked as a modifier and summary element.

flags.isModifierReason: This element is labeled as a modifier because once a practitioner is marked as deceased, the record should only be used/retained for historical purposes.

semanticText.definition: Indicates if the practitioner is deceased or not.
semanticText.comment: If there is no value in the instance, it means there is no statement on whether or not the practitioner is deceased. Most systems will interpret the absence of a value as a sign of the person being alive.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 can directly state whether and when a practitioner is deceased, and the element changes safe use of the resource.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Adding an optional element does not invalidate R4 data moving forward, but R6 instances containing `deceasedBoolean` or `deceasedDateTime` are not representable in base R4 Practitioner. Because it is a modifier, dropping it during downgrade can cause downstream systems to treat historical/deceased practitioner records as normally usable.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Loss of deceased status can lead to inappropriate continued use of practitioner records in directories, routing, assignments, or historical attribution workflows.

justification.inferredGoal: Represent deceased practitioners directly and consistently with other person-like resources.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: No R4-to-R6 backward-compatible alternative is needed because the new element is optional and preserves R4 instances.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Representing deceased status directly is a reasonable R6 goal because it affects whether the Practitioner record should be used only historically. The addition does not invalidate R4 Practitioner instances moving to R6; the risk is that R6 instances containing the new modifier choice cannot be represented losslessly in base R4. Given the safety relevance, adding the optional modifier element is justified despite downgrade handling needs.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: This finding is not a breaking R4-to-R6 base-design issue: R4 instances remain valid with the optional R6 element absent. Using an R4 extension during downgrade is a migration mitigation, not a backward-compatible base R6 alternative. An extension-only R6 design would reduce R6-to-R4 round-trip friction, but it would also make a safety-relevant deceased status less visible to R6-native generic clients.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: The main tradeoff is R6-to-R4 downgrade loss, which requires an extension or policy but is not a less-breaking base R6 design alternative.

evidence.detail: No R4 snapshot element with id Practitioner.deceased[x].
R6 adds deceased[x] with boolean and dateTime types, cardinality 0..1, isModifier true, and isSummary true.

examples.examplesMd: The extension URL is illustrative only. A production downgrade should use an approved cross-version extension or local migration convention.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 adds a new modifier choice element for deceased status. Forward migration from R4 is not blocked because the element is optional, but downgrade and mixed-version processing are risky because this safety-relevant status has no R4 base location.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-to-R6: no old instance is invalidated by the addition. R6-to-R4: an R6 instance with `deceasedBoolean` or `deceasedDateTime` cannot be represented losslessly in base R4 and an R4 validator will reject the unknown base element unless it is transformed to an extension or removed. Removing it is semantically unsafe because the element is a modifier.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: When upgrading, leave absent unless source data has a known deceased fact. When downgrading, preserve the value using a cross-version or implementation-specific extension and ensure consumers understand it; do not silently drop it. Add tests for both boolean and dateTime forms and for workflows that should exclude deceased practitioners from active use.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The base addition is useful and probably justified, but it creates unavoidable R6-to-R4 loss unless a standard extension is used. A pure extension design would have been easier to backport but less safe for R6-native consumers.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Check whether the broader R6 cross-version extension set defines an official extension for this element before implementing downgrade transforms.

findings.title: R6 adds Practitioner.qualification.status

oldState.summary: R4 qualification had identifier, code, period, and issuer, but no status/progress element.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 could represent the qualification code and validity period, but not an explicit status such as in-progress, suspended, or revoked in the base resource.

newState.summary: Optional CodeableConcept status/progress element on each qualification with a preferred qualification-status value set.

semanticText.definition: Qualifications often take time to attain and might be tracked during this time, and completed qualifications might not always be valid.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 can explicitly carry qualification lifecycle state; the local CodeSystem includes codes such as active, inactive, in-progress, suspended, and revoked.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The optional addition does not invalidate R4 instances, but R6 data using `qualification.status` cannot be carried in a base R4 Practitioner without extension or lossy omission. The risk is meaningful when status conveys that a qualification is not yet usable, suspended, revoked, or only temporary.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Dropping revoked, suspended, or in-progress status can misrepresent practitioner authorization or credentialing state.

justification.inferredGoal: Represent qualification lifecycle state separately from validity period.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: No R4-to-R6 backward-compatible alternative is needed because this is an optional R6 addition.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Qualification status captures lifecycle information that `period` and `code` do not reliably express, including suspended, revoked, pending, or in-progress states. Because the element is optional, non-modifier, and does not invalidate R4 instances on upgrade, the base R6 addition is justified. The compatibility concern is mainly loss of information when converting R6 data back to base R4.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: This is not an R4-to-R6 breaking base-design issue under the calibration rules. Existing R4 `Practitioner.qualification` entries can migrate without populating `status`; only R6 data that chooses to use the new field needs downgrade handling. Carrying the value in an R4 extension is a reasonable conversion strategy, but it is not a backward-compatible alternative to a forward-breaking R6 design.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: R6-to-R4 conversion may need an extension or lossy omission, but that is downgrade mitigation rather than an alternative to an R4-to-R6 break.

evidence.detail: No R4 snapshot element with id Practitioner.qualification.status.
R6 adds status as 0..1 CodeableConcept with preferred binding to qualification-status.
The R6 qualification-status CodeSystem includes active, inactive, in-progress, pending, temporary, conditional, suspended, and revoked.

examples.examplesMd: The extension URL is illustrative. Production R6-to-R4 conversion should use an approved cross-version extension if available.

findings.narrativeMd: `Practitioner.qualification.status` is a new R6 base element. It is not a forward validation break, but it is important for downgrade and credentialing workflows because R4 had no equivalent base element for status/progress separate from `period`.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-to-R6: no old instance is invalidated by the optional addition. R6-to-R4: an R6 instance with `qualification.status` is not base-R4-representable and will need an extension or lossy drop. The binding is preferred, so non-value-set codes are not a hard validation failure by themselves.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For upgrade, populate status only when source data distinguishes qualification lifecycle state from period. For downgrade, preserve status in an extension and review credentialing/business rules before dropping values such as `suspended` or `revoked`. Test status plus period combinations.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The addition is reasonable because status and validity period answer different questions. It could have been extension-only to ease backporting, but first-class modeling is useful for credentialing interoperability.

checkedNoMaterialChange.notesMd: The canonical URL, id, name, kind, type, abstract flag, derivation, and DomainResource base identity are stable. The R4 status `draft` changed to R6 `active`, but that is not an instance or code-generation break for Practitioner identity.
No pre-existing local Practitioner element had a min or max cardinality change. New optional elements and new child cardinalities are covered in findings.
No Practitioner-specific invariant was added, removed, or materially changed. Differences seen for dom-* and ele-1 constraints are inherited from base artifacts and excluded from local findings.
No local Practitioner element gained or lost fixed, pattern, or default values in the compared StructureDefinitions.
No local maxLength, minValue, maxValue, or regex limits changed for Practitioner elements.
No local Practitioner slicing changes were found.
Summary flags on pre-existing local elements are stable. R6 adds `deceased[x]` as a summary element, and inherited `modifierExtension` summary changes are out of scope.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Qualification code example binding changed from versioned v2-2.7-0360 to unversioned v2-0360
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The binding strength remains `example`, so base validation should not reject instances solely because they use codes outside the referenced value set. This is therefore not a hard instance-breaking change.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Terminology-driven UI picklists, examples, or local profiles that assumed the R4 version-specific value set may need review. The R6 core package did not include a local `ValueSet-v2-0360.json` file in the same way R4 included `ValueSet-v2-2.7-0360.json`, so terminology resolution may depend on the terminology package/server.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Administrative gender required binding version changed but codes remained stable
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The binding remains required to administrative-gender, and the local R4 and R6 CodeSystems both contain the same four codes: male, female, other, and unknown.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Implementations that compare canonical URLs including version should update from `|4.0.1` to `|6.0.0-ballot4`, but instance code values do not need a mapping based on the inspected core CodeSystems.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: StructureDefinition status changed from draft to active
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The artifact remains the same canonical non-abstract resource specialization. Maturity/status metadata does not change Practitioner instance wire format.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Governance and dependency tooling may treat the R6 artifact as active rather than draft.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Root definition broadens wording to healthcare or related services
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The root definition change appears to broaden or clarify scope rather than invalidate old Practitioner instances.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Policy or directory systems with strict definitions of practitioner scope may want to review the broader R6 wording.

followUpDependencies.reasonMd: R6 Practitioner.communication directs patient-facing language publication to PractitionerRole.communication. A PractitionerRole report should own the target element comparison and any role-specific migration rules.
Required binding impact for `Practitioner.communication.language` depends on terminology expansion and BCP 47 validation behavior.
R6 `Practitioner.qualification.status` uses this preferred value set; downstream migration may need a ConceptMap or local credentialing map.
The Practitioner snapshot reflects inherited DomainResource constraint expression changes, especially dom-3, but those are intentionally excluded from this local Practitioner report.
Inherited ele-1/ext-1 wording and extension constraint differences appear in the snapshot but should be analyzed by the base artifact reports.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: Terminology analysis used local ValueSet and CodeSystem JSON only. No live expansion or validation was run for BCP 47 language tags, v2-0360, or qualification-status.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Run a terminology server expansion/validation for the exact R4 and R6 value sets and compare accepted codes and text-only CodeableConcept behavior.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: The assessment did not use official R4-to-R6 diff pages, Jira issues, ballot notes, or committee rationale, so backward-compatibility and justification judgements are inferred from the computable definitions.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Review the official spec narrative, change notes, and issue history for Practitioner and PractitionerRole.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: The report did not survey implementation guides, production examples, or real-world datasets, so expected prevalence is expert judgement rather than measured frequency.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Sample R4 Practitioner instances and common IG profiles to measure actual use of communication, active=false, deceased extensions, and qualification lifecycle data.
